title: Connect the four financial statements
purpose: Trace one transaction through profit, assets, equity, and cash.
concept: Transactions can affect several statements at once. Earning revenue is different from collecting cash; paying a dividend reduces equity without reducing profit.
formula: Ending retained earnings = beginning retained earnings + net income − dividends
connection: A monthly close is a connected reconciliation. An entry should explain both where value sits and how it got there.
trap: Owner funding is financing, not revenue. A dividend is a distribution, not an expense.

title: Separate earning, paying, and collecting
purpose: Choose the period that receives the service or earns the revenue.
concept: Payment, delivery, and recognition can occur in different periods. A prepayment remains an asset until consumed; an advance remains a liability until earned.
formula: Unconsumed prepayment = cash paid − expense recognized
connection: At close, ask what was delivered or consumed this month before asking when the bank moved.
trap: Cash received is not automatically revenue, and cash paid is not automatically expense.

title: Explain why profit is not operating cash
purpose: Build an indirect operating cash bridge without reversing the signs.
concept: Start with net income. Remove noncash expense effects and adjust operating working capital for cash timing. Keep investing and financing separate.
formula: CFO = net income + depreciation − increase in receivables − increase in inventory + increase in payables
connection: This is the same bridge you would use to explain why a profitable month still required borrowing.
trap: Depreciation is added back because it reduced profit without using current cash. The addback is not a cash receipt.

title: Recognize revenue as the service is delivered
purpose: Separate an advance payment from earned revenue in a simple contract.
concept: A valid customer contract identifies promised performance. Revenue follows satisfaction of that obligation, not simply a payment or invoice.
formula: Earned revenue = contract price × measured performance satisfied
connection: A customer paying early helps cash; it does not mean the team has completed its work.
trap: This example qualifies for recognition over time because the customer receives and consumes benefits as work occurs. A calendar alone is not evidence.

title: Follow inventory cost into profit and valuation
purpose: Explain how cost assignment changes ending inventory and gross profit.
concept: Costs of goods available must end up in cost of goods sold or ending inventory. Periodic FIFO and weighted average assign different costs; a valuation check comes afterward.
formula: Goods available cost = cost of goods sold + ending inventory (before write-down)
connection: Use the rollforward to explain a margin movement before treating it as an operating improvement.
trap: Cost flow is an accounting assumption. This lesson covers periodic FIFO and weighted average under the lower-of-cost-and-NRV rule, not LIFO or the retail method.

title: Estimate receivable losses without double-counting
purpose: Adjust the allowance to its required balance, then trace a write-off.
concept: An allowance reduces gross receivables to an expected collectible amount. Adjust the existing allowance to the required ending balance; a later write-off uses the allowance.
formula: Net receivables = gross receivables − allowance; adjustment = required allowance − existing credit balance
connection: A collections issue affects both the balance sheet estimate and profit. A write-off should not record the same expected loss again.
trap: The expected loss rate is given for this exercise. It is not a universal rule for estimating credit losses.
